workflow: Follow a strict 4-phase workflow within your 40-step budget: (1) Understand (5-10 steps): locate relevant files by searching for error messages, function names, or keywords from the issue description; read only the files that directly relate to the reported problem. (2) Validate Understanding (mandatory checkpoint): before making ANY edit, explicitly state in your thought section: ROOT CAUSE (one-sentence bug description), EXACT LOCATION (file path and line numbers), and SPECIFIC EDIT (what you will change). (3) Execute Fix (1 step): make ONE precise edit using sed or cat with heredoc to fix the identified issue. (4) Submit IMMEDIATELY (1 step): run `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT` as a standalone command without combining it with anything else. Do NOT run tests, do NOT verify your changes, do NOT re-read files after editing—submit right after the fix.
context_strategy: Keep your conversation history focused on the direct path to the bug. If you have read more than 5 files without identifying the exact bug location, STOP exploring and re-read the original issue description to refocus your search. Avoid wandering through tangentially related code. Each step should build directly toward stating the three checkpoint items (root cause, exact location, specific edit). Once you have made your edit, do not retain or review verification thoughts—your next message must be the submit command.
submission_strategy: Before submitting, verify in your final thought that you have: (1) stated the ROOT CAUSE in one sentence, (2) identified the EXACT LOCATION (file and line numbers), (3) described the SPECIFIC EDIT you made, and (4) actually executed that edit with a sed or cat command. Do NOT verify the edit by re-reading the file, do NOT run any tests (pytest, manage.py test, or any test execution command), and do NOT check for syntax errors. Submit immediately after editing—the submission command must be issued alone, not combined with any other command.
hints: The repository structure varies by issue, so start by listing the current directory and searching for keywords from the issue (use grep -r or find). When editing, always view the exact line numbers first (use nl -ba filename | sed -n 'start,endp') before running sed to ensure line numbers are correct. On macOS, use 'sed -i ""' instead of 'sed -i'. Most bugs require only a single-line or few-line change in one file. Test files are rarely the correct edit target (less than 3% of successful fixes). If the issue mentions a specific error message, search the codebase for that exact string to locate the source. Directory and environment changes do not persist between commands, so prefix commands with 'cd /path && ...' if needed.
budget_guidance: Allocate your 40 steps as follows: 5-10 steps for exploration and understanding (finding files, reading relevant code sections), 0 steps for the mandatory checkpoint (this is part of your thought process, not a separate action), 1 step for making the edit, 1 step for submitting. This leaves you 28-34 steps of buffer—do NOT use this buffer for testing or verification, use it only if your initial exploration needs to go slightly deeper. The median successful trajectory completes in 18-20 steps. If you approach 25 steps without having made an edit, you are likely wandering—refocus immediately. Never spend steps on running tests (pytest, test commands), re-reading edited files, or checking syntax. The dominant failure mode is running out of steps before submitting, not submitting wrong fixes.
